lines: The AI wrote workspace B on its request. The server crossed it out.
To save a memory, an AI sends two ids: the message it came from, and its chat. Nothing ties them. One wrong guess, or one buggy client, and a real message lands in the wrong chat.
Both ids come from the same writer. Only the server's records know which chat that message is in.

So the server stops asking. The model sends the message id. The server looks it up in its own records and stamps the chat from there. Same rule for the workspace: it comes from who's signed in. Put B in the request, and the write still lands in A.
One real memory tool asks for six fields, all required. Chat id isn't one of them. Its description says why: derived on the server.
It won't prove the AI picked the right message. It stops one thing: that message in the wrong chat. Let the model choose. Make the server decide.
facts: Sources: devweb.org/articles/skills-subagents-mcp-where-logic-lives (devweb content/articles/skills-subagents-mcp-where-logic-lives.mdx) and devweb.org/articles/mcp-tool-design (mcp-tool-design.mdx); the workspace beat from the systems repo's storage-routing test (candidates-systems S12). I: S12, a dispatch whose payload names workspace B 'lands its write in workspace A (the context's) and leaves B unchanged'; routing comes 'from the authenticated context and from nothing a caller supplies'. II: where-logic-lives, 'the caller would supply a source-turn identifier but not a separate chat identifier' and the hazard it removes, a caller that could 'send a source-turn identifier and independently pair it with an arbitrary chat_id'; 'It does not stop a buggy or hostile client from sending inconsistent identifiers.' The model's guess: mcp-tool-design, chat_id is required on chat_log_turn and chat_recent, 'so a model that has learned the rest of this surface has decent reason to think it belongs here too.' III: where-logic-lives, 'The server would look up the source turn and derive chat_id from it.' IV: same, plus 'server-derived identifiers' as an enforcement at the data-owning boundary; workspace from the signed-in context per S12. V: mcp-tool-design, 'The inputSchema for write_memory declares six properties and requires all six. chat_id is not among them.' and the description line 'chat_id is NOT an input — it is derived server-side from source_turn_id.' VI: where-logic-lives, 'It would not prove the caller chose the right source turn' and 'name the exact failure it stops, and no more'; 'Let the model choose among safe actions. Reject unsafe states at a boundary the model cannot waive.' Not claimed: tenant isolation or per-user authorization from the chat_id derivation (the article says it does not establish them). Ep02 covered 'a prompt rule is a request'; this one is the server deriving identity and scope from its own record. Title: 'Telling the AI to be careful isn't a security rule.' (episodes.md #30, D25, folds in #75/S12).
